description: We are a research-driven student team competing in "The Earth Information Jukebox" challenge.
summary:
The NASA Space Apps Challenge, “The Earth Information Jukebox,” asks participants to make complex Earth science more engaging and accessible by transforming visual information into sound. It explores how sonification, the use of non-speech audio to represent data, can help people experience and understand our changing planet beyond visual charts and images.

To address this challenge, we developed SonifyEarth, an interactive web experience that combines NASA Earth visualization context with dynamically generated sound based on quality-controlled ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor (ISS LIS) V2.2 observations.

Our sound design represents three scientific states with distinct audio cues: DETECTED uses short percussive pulses, OBSERVED_NO_DETECTION creates a sustained observation texture, and UNKNOWN uses a neutral two-part cue. Users can explore the historical observations through an interactive map and timeline and choose between two listening modes: EVENT-ONLY and OBSERVATION-AWARE. The “Why Did I Hear That?” feature explains the evidence behind each sound.

SonifyEarth turns satellite observations into an interactive listening experience, offering another way to explore Earth science while making the distinction between detection, non-detection, and uncertainty clear.
details:
What does the project do and how does it work?

SonifyEarth is an interactive web application developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, specifically the challenge “The Earth Information Jukebox.” The challenge encourages participants to make complex Earth science more engaging and accessible by transforming visual information into sound.

Our project uses quality-controlled NASA ISS Lightning Imaging Sensor (ISS LIS) V2.2 Science and Backgrounds data to create an interactive listening experience. The processed historical observations are presented through an interactive map and timeline, alongside NASA Earth visualization context.

SonifyEarth identifies three scientific states:

  • DETECTED: Lightning was detected during a valid observation.
  • OBSERVED_NO_DETECTION: The satellite observed the area, but no lightning was detected.
  • UNKNOWN: The area or period cannot be confidently classified because of coverage limitations, data gaps, or observation-quality issues.

The sound engine translates these states into distinct audio cues. DETECTED produces short percussive pulses, OBSERVED_NO_DETECTION creates a sustained observation texture, and UNKNOWN uses a neutral two-part cue.

Users can explore the data through two listening modes: EVENT-ONLY, which focuses on detected lightning events, and OBSERVATION-AWARE, which provides a broader listening experience that includes observation context. The “Why Did I Hear That?” evidence inspector explains the data and reasoning behind the sounds.

What benefits does it have?

SonifyEarth offers another way to experience satellite observations beyond conventional visual maps and charts. It helps users explore when lightning was detected, when observations occurred without a detection, and when the available data is uncertain.

It also makes the sound meaningful rather than purely decorative by connecting audio cues to documented scientific states.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make Earth science more engaging, understandable, and accessible through sound. We hope SonifyEarth can encourage students, educators, researchers, and the wider public to explore satellite data through a different sensory experience, including people who benefit from audio-based information.

What tools and technologies did we use?

  • Python: Data processing, scientific checks, state classification, and preparation of data for the website.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: Website structure, styling, interactive interface, map, and timeline.
  • Web Audio API: Real-time browser-based sound generation and playback.
  • JSON and GeoJSON: Structured data and geographic information used by the website.
  • NetCDF and HDF: NASA satellite data formats used during data inspection and processing.
  • NASA ISS LIS V2.2 Science and Backgrounds datasets: The scientific data foundation.
  • NASA SVS 5011: Earth visualization context for the experience.

The experience runs in a web browser and does not require dedicated audio hardware.

How is the project creative?

Instead of simply playing background music, SonifyEarth uses scientific observation states to shape its sound design. Its central idea is that silence does not always mean nothing happened. A period with no detected lightning can still represent a meaningful satellite observation, while an unobserved or uncertain period must remain distinguishable.

The two listening modes let users experience the same data from different perspectives, while the evidence inspector connects each sound to its scientific explanation.

What factors did our team consider?

We prioritized scientific accuracy, data quality, satellite observation coverage, uncertainty, timestamp handling, and the distinction between non-detection and missing observation. We also considered usability and accessibility through keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, text equivalents, clear state descriptions, and no automatic audio playback.

The sound design was developed to communicate data meaning without presenting uncertain observations as confirmed scientific events.
